extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent drafters, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for determining the permissible scope of patent claims, what constitutes a patentable application of a discovery, and the proper drafting and recording formalities for specifications and assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery vs invention: must connect discovery to particular means
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery of a new principle, force, or law, operating or which can be made to operate on matter, will not entitle the discoverer to a patent. It is only where the discoverer has gone beyond mere discovery and has connected the new principle, force, or law with some particular medium or mechanical contrivance by which, or through which, it acts on the material world, that he can secure the exclusive control of it under the patent laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The discoverer controls the discovery only through the means by which he has brought it into practical action (or their equivalents). Sever the principle from the means and it becomes a 'naked discovery' not subject to patent monopoly. Example: the court held the discovery of ether's anesthetic effect was not patentable as a naked discovery; only its application via described means could be patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim abstract principles; claims must have application/conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that presents a principle or motive-power merely as a cause of a result, divorced from the conditions and practical means of its application, is void as an abstraction (illustrated by O'Reilly v. Morse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General claims that 'divest[] [the invention] of all conditions' are void. A valid claim must define the conditions and practical means that link cause to effect; otherwise it overreaches and is invalidated as an abstract appropriation of a principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must describe means 'full and exact' so skilled person can produce result
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must specify the means he uses 'in a manner so full and exact, that any one skilled in the science to which it appertains can, by using the means he specifies, without any addition to or subtraction from them, produce precisely the result he describes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the result cannot be produced by the means described, the patent is void. If it can, the patent confers exclusive right only over the use of those means. This is a test for sufficiency of disclosure: enablement and completeness of specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of patent limited to means described and their equivalents within the inventor's conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specification furnishes means of making the application, the patentee's exclusive right is to use the means he specifies to produce the described effect, and nothing more; others may accomplish the same end if they use means 'substantially different' from those described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the method or rule of action can be effected by various agents, the limits of the patent are defined by the function those means discharge relative to the method. Determine equivalents relative to the method/rule of action embodied by the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial difference or identity of means is tested by function and method, not external form
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial difference of means does not depend upon differences of form, structure, composition, or other external variations, so long as the method or rule of action embraced by the patent remains unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases where the invention's rule of action is embodied in particular devices, test infringement by asking whether the accused means perform the same function in the performance of that method; mere external variations do not avoid infringement if the method remains unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims giving conditions of application can validly embrace various devices
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conditions of the application of a principle are given and means of making it are furnished, the claim is not necessarily void; the inventor may define conditions which form the limits of his invention, and those conditions may embrace many devices or forms differing from those used by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Neilson's patent (hot blast) was upheld because he gave conditions admitting various heating apparatus. The key is to ascertain and articulate the conditions limiting the asserted invention so the scope is not merely conjectural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid separating the principle from necessary means in drafting (draft to the application by means)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid claiming an abstract principle, the specification and claims should use appropriate terms signifying that the application of the principle is claimed as effected by the means used and described by the patentee and by all other means which, applied within the just scope of his conditions, will perform the like office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No universal formula of words exists; formularies are of little use. Use language that ties the claimed application to concrete means and to equivalents within the stated conditions. Anti-pattern: drafting broad language that purports to claim a principle irrespective of implementation (e.g., Morse's overly general claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims must recite the process/means, not merely the desired result
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim that merely names the result (e.g., 'rendering the system insensible to pain') without specifying anything beyond a well-known, ordinary process (e.g., inhalation of vapor) is not a patentable process; coupling a result to a known means does not create patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process must include novel or particular steps or instruments beyond the ordinary function to be patentable. Claiming only the effect produced by old agents and old means is insufficient. Draft process claims to recite the operative steps or new mode of application.

rubrics_metrics.name: New or more perfect effect by known agents/known means is insufficient for patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A new or additional effect produced by old agents operating by old means upon old subjects — for example, producing insensibility by inhalation of ether in greater quantity — is not sufficient to support a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements that are merely a better or more perfect use of a known agent by known means (where the change is a matter of operator discretion or quantity) generally do not meet patentability requirements unless embodied in a novel means or method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of claim depends on inventor's disclosure and position in order of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor who gives conditions that admit application of a principle by various means (and who stands in the order of invention to justify such a claim) may legitimately claim the broader application; conversely, a general claim that is unlimited as to conditions (as in Morse) is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the patentee provided the necessary conditions or rule of action to support a broader claim; if not, the claim should be restricted to what the patentee truly described and enabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments before patent issue: formal requisites and effect on legal title
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes permit issuance of a patent to an assignee provided an assignment is recorded and the application and specification are duly made and sworn to by the inventor. If an instrument executed before issuance contemplates the patent issuing to the inventor, the holder of the instrument may have only an equitable title until the legal formality is met; but an assignment recorded before issue that requests the patent to issue to the assignee may operate as a legal assignment even if the patent later issues in the inventor's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical requisites: record the assignment in the Patent Office (ideally before or at the time of application), ensure the specification and application are made in the inventor's name and sworn, and evidence intent whether the patent should issue to assignee or inventor. Failure to observe statutory recording/formalities can leave assignees with only equitable rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inchoate or incomplete inventions are not assignable as legal title
rubrics_metrics.description: There can properly be no assignment of an inchoate or incomplete invention; a contract to convey a future invention may be valid and enforced, but the legal title to an invention passes only by a conveyance operating upon the thing invented after it has become capable of being the subject of an application for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties wish to transfer rights before patenting, use clear written instruments and be aware that, absent statutory formality and a perfected invention, the transferee usually holds equitable rather than legal title until patent procedures are completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment by operation of law (e.g., bankruptcy) passes patent interest where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments by act or operation of law (such as bankruptcy) divest the patentee of property and pass the patent interest with the rest of the estate. This is certainly true of a patent already issued before the assignment; in some jurisdictions/pieces of authority, a patent issued after bankruptcy but before the bankrupt obtains a certificate has been held to pass to the assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that statutory and jurisdictional rules govern when a patent interest passes by operation of law; check local precedent for treatment of patents issuing during pending insolvency proceedings.
